records.prose: The 1117 class uses the output capacitor as loop compensation, so both a minimum C and an ESR window are requirements. Subject datasheet (AMS1117, Application Hints / Stability, p4): the circuit design "requires the use of an output capacitor as part of the device frequency compensation"; 22 uF solid tantalum "will ensure stability for all operating conditions"; bypassing ADJ raises the requirement and 22 uF tantalum covers all cases; larger values only improve stability. It publishes NO numeric ESR window. TI's LM1117 (same 1117 family) quantifies it (s9.2.2.1.3, p15): minimum 10 uF if tantalum, ESR between 0.3 and 22 ohm, 22 uF tantalum when CADJ is used - disagreement on minimum C (10 vs 22 uF) resolved toward the subject part's own 22 uF blanket figure. A bare X5R/X7R ceramic has mohm-level ESR (AN-1482 s6), far BELOW the 0.3 ohm floor: a "same 22 uF" ceramic substitution can push the loop out of its stable region. Use tantalum / polymer with in-window ESR, or a ceramic plus deliberate series resistance, and re-verify. This board's committed 22 uF tantalum-class output cap is exactly the datasheet path - GROUNDED. Contrast: ceramic- stable CMOS LDOs invert the rule - Diodes AP2112 is "Stable with 1.0 uF Flexible Cap: Ceramic, Tantalum and Aluminum Electrolytic" (p1) with 1 uF X5R/X7R in/out in the typical application (p2 Note 4).

records.prose: What the family datasheets actually require at VIN: the subject AMS1117 datasheet states NO input-capacitor value or ESR condition anywhere in its Application Hints (p4 shows an unlabeled cap at VIN in Fig 2 only) - CIN is not stability-critical for this family, the ESR window belongs to COUT. The TI LM1117 sibling makes the requirement explicit: "An input capacitor is recommended. A 10-uF tantalum on the input is a suitable input capacitor for almost all applications" (s9.2.2.1.1, p14), and the Fig 9-3 fixed-regulator example marks its 10 uF tantalum CIN "Required if the regulator is located far from the power supply filter" (p16) - the cap's job is local source impedance, so it sits at the VIN pin and becomes mandatory when upstream bulk is not adjacent. Layout per LM1117 9.5.1 (p17): load-current traces wide (parasitic inductance); VOUT-to-ADJ feedback loop as short as possible; ADJ bypass as close as possible to the IC; and when VIN can be shorted to ground, a diode from VOUT to VIN placed close to the pins diverts the output-cap surge. AMS1117 p4 bounds the same risk: the internal diode absorbs 50-100 A microsecond surges, and the external diode is recommended only with very large COUT (1000-5000 uF) or an input crowbar - not needed at 22 uF scale.

rule.check: Vsource_worst_low - sum(series drops at Iout) >= Vout + Vdropout_max(Iout, Tj)
rule.corner: source worst-case LOW x Iout max x dropout MAX spec

records.prose: Everything in series ahead of the LDO input subtracts from dropout headroom: PTC/polyfuse resistance, connector and cable contact resistance, input filter and trace resistance, any ORing diode. The check is run at the SOURCE's worst-case low corner with the dropout MAX spec at the real load - never at nominals. Dropout is load- and temperature-dependent: AMS1117 specs 1.1 V typ / 1.3 V max at 0.8 A, and Note 4 warns dropout is HIGHER above 0.8 A and unspecified there (p3); LM1117 Fig 9-2 shows the curve - roughly 1.0-1.15 V rising with load at Tj 25 C, lower at 125 C (p15) - and TI 9.4 says the minimum dropout "must also be met with extra headroom when possible" (p17). Worked at this class of operating point: Vout 3.3 + 1.3 max = 4.6 V required by the family's own max spec; ~1.1 V typ at 0.3 A gives 4.4 V. From a nominal 5.0 V USB source that leaves only 0.4-0.6 V for ALL series elements before the VBUS low corner is even counted, and every 100 mohm of PTC+connector resistance at 0.3 A eats another 30 mV. If the budget does not close, the fix is a genuinely low-dropout class - e.g. CMOS AP2112: 250 mV typ at 600 mA (p1) - or a different topology; a bigger thermal pour does not buy headroom.

rule.stable_window: part-published ESR band - BOTH boundaries matter

records.prose: The LDO output capacitor is a loop component, not just a reservoir: its ESR forms a zero at f = 1/(2*pi*ESR*Cout). In classic LDOs the loop counts on that zero for phase lead - AN-1482 Fig 4 (gain/phase plot) shows a 10 uF / 0.5 ohm tantalum's 30 kHz zero lifting phase margin from 11 to 68 deg. That is why such parts publish a stable ESR RANGE with two boundaries (Fig 6: an electrolytic-stable LDO's measured stable region, roughly 0.1 to 10 ohm at Cout 4.7 uF across 0-200 mA): too-high ESR puts the zero too low and over-extends bandwidth; too-low ESR pushes the zero past crossover and the loop oscillates. Ceramics have mohm-level ESR (a 10 uF ceramic's zero lands above 3 MHz - s6), so a bare low-ESR ceramic can sit OUTSIDE an ESR-zero part's stable region. Ceramic-stable LDOs instead build the zero into the error amp (Fig 5, series Rcomp): minimum stable ESR drops to ~0 but the MAXIMUM drops too (~0.5 ohm, Fig 7) - the capacitor requirement inverts between the two design eras. Corollary (s7/Fig 8): small 0.01-0.1 uF ceramics sprinkled on the rail add a pole; 1 uF of ceramic bypass dropped a 68 deg margin to 9 deg. Never swap output-cap type against the part's stated stability conditions, and keep stray small ceramics away from the output terminal (s8).

records.prose: A linear regulator's usable output current on a given board is set by thermal resistance and copper area, NOT by the datasheet headline current: check Tj = Ta(max) + PD*thetaJA <= 125 C, PD = (Vin-Vout)*Iout (AMS1117 p5 gives the pair; LM1117 p18 adds Vin*Ignd and the inverse RthetaJA_allowed = (125-Ta)/PD). thetaJA is a board property tied to the SOT-223 tab pour. At the minimum-copper end the sources disagree: TI LM1117 p18 Table 9-2 row 1 measures 136 C/W (0.0123 in2 top, 0 bottom); AMS's 90 C/W headline is an unqualified nameplate - its own p2 footnote concedes phi-JA varies 46 to >90 C/W with mounting and copper size even over a backside/internal plane. Budget minimal copper at the measured 136 C/W. With real pours the vendors converge: TI Table 9-2 / Fig 9-11 - 0.3 in2 -> 84, 1 in2 top 1 oz -> 66, flattening past ~0.5 in2; AMS p5 Table 1 (1/16 in FR-4, 1 oz) - 2500+2500 mm2 top+back -> 55, 1000 mm2 top -> 65, 100 mm2 top + 2500 back -> 80; junction-to-tab is 15 C/W and the spreading layer need not be electrically connected. AMS's 'as low as 45 C/W' is its optimistic corner - size the pour from a table row you can actually place. At 0.51 W a bare footprint at 136 C/W costs a 69 C rise; a real tab pour at 55-66 C/W costs 28-34 C - the pour IS the design margin. AMS1117 p3 Note 2: regulation guaranteed only to 1.2 W in SOT-223; TI Fig 9-15 (p20): allowable PD tops out near 1.5 W (1 in2, 25 C still air).

rule.networks_total: exactly one 100 nF + one 4.7 uF across pins 4/5 (TSSOP-20)

records.prose: Family rule (STM32G0x0 packages without separate analog supply pins): the whole decoupling requirement collapses to ONE 100 nF + ONE 4.7 uF network across the single bonded supply pin pair - no VDDA or VREF+ network is possible or needed. DS12991 3.7.1 (read p.14): VDDA "voltage level is identical to VDD ... provided externally through VDD/VDDA pin"; when no VBAT pin exists "VBAT bonding pad is internally bonded to the VDD/VDDA pin"; p.15: "On packages without VREF+ pin, VREF+ is internally connected with VDD." Table 12 (read p.31): on TSSOP-20 pin 4 is the only supply (VDD/VDDA, type S) and pin 5 the only ground (VSS/VSSA); VBAT and VREF+ rows exist only in the LQFP48 column (its pins 4/5). Fig 9 (read p.39) draws ST's network: '1 x 100 nF + 1 x 4.7 uF' on VDD/VDDA, and a separate 100 nF on VREF+ that only applies to packages exposing VREF+; caution: place as close as possible to, or below, the pins. Consequence for layout: one two-cap group tight to pins 4/5, sharing the shortest ground return. Trade-off to carry forward (cross-vendor, AN2519 2.2 read p.6): a separate analog supply pin exists on other packages precisely so analog circuits escape digital switching noise and get their own decoupling - on bonded packages the ADC shares the digital rail, so noise-critical analog work argues for a package with a true VDDA pin, not extra caps.

rule.hf_bypass_per: supply pin pair (VDD/VSS), one cap per pair
rule.placement: as close as the package allows; minimize cap-pin-gnd loop area; opposite side of board acceptable for this

records.prose: Principle: an MCU draws its supply current in short spikes on clock and I/O edges; spikes cannot be delivered over long supply lines, so the decoupling capacitor is the source - one HF ceramic (100 nF is both vendors' value here) per supply pin pair, placed as close as the package allows so the cap->VDD->VSS->cap loop is minimal, plus one bulk cap per device to stabilize the rail. AN2519 Fig 2-1 (read p.5) draws the failure: a cap placed far away enlarges the high-current loop, the power/ground planes join the loop and the whole ground plane acts as an antenna, raising radiated emission. P.6 (Fig 2-2 read): connect the cap as close as possible to the power and ground pins - for large packages the opposite side of the board may get it closest - it is critical to minimize the loop area between cap and pins; for devices with multiple power/ground pin pairs "there is a decoupling capacitor for every pair of pins"; the main supply "should also have a tantalum or ceramic capacitor to stabilize it". ST states the same for the subject part: DS12991 Fig 9 caution (read p.39) - decouple the supply pin pair with the shown ceramics "as close as possible to, or below, the appropriate pins on the underside of the PCB"; p.70 General PCB design guidelines - the 100 nF must be good-quality ceramic, as close as possible to the chip.

records.prose: Crystal-less operation is a budget comparison: the internal RC's total accuracy (trim + temperature + supply drift) against the clock-tolerance budget of each clocked interface. Subject-part numbers, DS12991 Table 38 (read p.54-55): HSI16 factory-trimmed to 15.88-16.08 MHz at 30 C / 3.0 V (-0.75/+0.5 pct); drift +-1 pct over 0..85 C, -2/+1.5 pct over -40..85 C, -0.1/+0.05 pct over VDD; start-up 1.2 us max, stabilization 5 us max. Worst-case sum 0..85 C is about -1.85/+1.55 pct. The UART budget, cross-vendor (AVR16EA DS 25.3.3.2.3, Tables 25-4/25-5, read): the recommended maximum receiver baud-rate error - assuming transmitter and receiver split the total error equally - is +-2.0 pct for a D=8 frame (8N1) in 16x-oversampling mode, tightening to +-1.5 pct at D=10 and in 8x (double-speed) mode. Verdict for the class: an RC-clocked UART at a standard baud rate is acceptable against a crystal-timed link partner over 0..85 C (RC error stays inside the +-2 pct half-budget, with little margin at the extremes); it is marginal at industrial cold (-40 C blows the 8N1 budget on drift alone) and when BOTH ends run on RC (they consume the whole split). Interfaces whose specified clock tolerance is tighter than the RC spec - USB full-speed is the canonical case - are out of reach without a crystal or a closed-loop trim source; not live here (G030 has no USB peripheral). Longer frames (parity, 9-bit) tighten the budget one step.

records.prose: For the STM32G030, ST's documented reset network needs no external pull-up: NRST 'is connected to a permanent pull-up resistor, RPU' (DS12991 5.3.15 + Table 52, read p.65: 25-55 kohm, typ 40; <70 ns pulses filtered, >350 ns resets). Fig 19 (read p.66): internal RPU on-chip; ONE dashed 'External reset circuit' block holds the push-button AND the 0.1 uF cap to GND (button straight across the cap, no series R); notes: external circuit must pull NRST below VIL(NRST)max = 0.3 x VDDIO1; the cap 'must be placed as close as possible to the device'. 3.7.2 (read p.15): integrated POR/PDR, 'without the need for an external reset circuit'; 3.7.5 (read p.17) qualifies 'permanent' - the pull-up is deactivated when the reset source is internal. This is ST practice, NOT cross-vendor: Microchip's AN2519 (read p.7) documents the opposite for AVR - the internal pull-up 'can be insufficient' in noisy environments; an external pull-up (>= 4.7 kohm; >= 10 kohm for DebugWIRE) is recommended (Fig 3-1), plus an ESD/Zener diode Reset-to-Vcc when HVPP is unused. Debug caveat: AN2519 p7 says only that the reset cap 'cannot be used when DebugWIRE or PDI is used'. The G030 pages read show no NRST debug constraint; none sourced for SWD. Cap sizing: fit ST's 100 nF; AN2519's Fig 3-1 note calls its R/C 'typical values' that 'must be changed accordingly'. Cross-vendor practice only, not ST's: AN2519 3.1 (read p.8) puts ~330 ohm between button and cap to limit the L*di/dt spike when the switch shorts the cap.

records.prose: Pull-up sizing for a sensor I2C bus that leaves the board on a cable (Qwiic/STEMMA-QT, ~0.5 m). Floor: UM10204 p50 Eq 2, Rp(min) = (VDD - VOL(max)) / IOL with the spec sink of 3 mA at VOL 0.4 V for VDD > 2 V (Table 10, p43): at 3.3 V that is (3.3-0.4)/3 mA ~ 970 ohm for interop with any compliant device. The SHT4x's own laxer floor is 390 ohm at VDD >= 1.62 V (DS Table 4, p9). Ceiling: UM10204 p50 Eq 1, Rp(max) = tr / (0.8473 x Cb); tr max is 1000 ns Standard, 300 ns Fast, 120 ns Fm+ and Cb max 400 pF (Table 11, p44). Application: Cb is the TOTAL of traces, pins, cable and downstream device, and the ceiling must hold at the TOP of the Cb budget - at 400 kHz Eq 1 is Rp(max)[kohm] ~ 354/Cb[pF]: 2.36 k at 150 pF but only 1.77 k at 200 pF. For a ~0.5 m cable plus one remote node (150-200 pF budget) fit ~1.5 kohm: Eq 1 then holds to ~236 pF, margin over the whole budget, and it stays above the 970 ohm floor (~1.9 mA sink at 3.3 V). Re-derive 354/Cb for a different cable length rather than copying the value; past ~365 pF the 400 kHz window closes against the 970 floor entirely; a 100 kHz-only bus relaxes the ceiling ~3.3x (tr 1000 ns). Fit the pull-ups once, at the host board; do not duplicate them on downstream nodes. Neither Sensirion nor the connector ecosystem publishes a pF/m figure for the Qwiic cable - estimate, then verify rise time at bring-up. DS p3 Fig 1 shows 10 kohm pull-ups: valid only for a short single-device bus, too high once a cable is added.

records.prose: PCB copper conduction, not air, is the dominant path carrying board self-heat into an RH/T sensor die. Design Guide sec 3 (p8, read visually): external heat sources raise the sensed temperature and depress the RH reading; in the extreme case at 90 pct RH a 1 degC deviation produces a 5 pct RH error - RH error is ~5x the temperature error at high humidity. Heat conduction from nearby sources (power electronics, microprocessors, displays) is called 'the more severe and most common source of temperature deviations' and 'mostly it occurs through the PCB'. Named mitigations: sufficient distance, removal of unnecessary metal around the sensor (trough milling or etching slits), and keeping metal connections on the PCB as thin as possible. Fig 8 panels: a) thin metal connections + distance = good; b) milled slits (white lines) around the sensor decrease conduction = good; c) thick metal connections = bad; d) heat source in close proximity = bad. DG sec 3.3 (p11): rule of thumb - implement the sensor as isolated from the device and as exposed to the environment as possible, best with ambient airflow; Fig 11 shows the three decoupling options: thin PCB connection tongue, milled slits, or a flex. States mechanism and direction only; nothing bounds it, so it is a principle.

records.prose: Layout rule set for the SHT4x block on a shared board. DS p16 Fig 17 (read visually): recommended land pattern, four 0.5 x 0.3 mm pads on a 1.4 x 0.8 mm grid; caption states 'There shall be no copper under the sensor other than at the pin pads.' DS p15 sec 5.3: do not solder the central die pad and do not place an exposed copper pad beneath it - it acts as a heat sink and prevents the heater from meeting spec. DS p17 Table 10: RthJA 246 K/W die-pad-soldered vs 297 K/W not-soldered (heater off; 308 vs 357 heater on) - Sensirion bolds the not-soldered columns as the recommended, higher-isolation configuration. DG p8 + p17: mitigate conduction by distance and removing unnecessary metal (milled/etched slits); DG Fig 17 worked example puts the sensor in a board corner with milled slits around it, a shielding wall and a housing opening for air exchange; Fig 18 simpler variant notes added PCB slits shield against external heating. Concrete rule: place the sensor on a board-edge/corner island reached only by its four necked traces (SDA, SCL, VDD, VSS), keep pours off the island, and mill a slot/slits across the remaining connection to break conduction from LDO/MCU. Sensirion publishes NO numeric mm slot width, trace width or clearance in DS/DG/HI - wording is qualitative ('as thin as possible', 'sufficient distances') - so mm values are designer judgement, not vendor numbers.

records.prose: DS p3 Fig 1 typical application circuit (read visually): the SHT4x carries one 100 nF capacitor from VDD to GND at the sensor, pull-ups on SDA/SCL, nothing else; text: after reaching minimal supply voltage and the maximal power-up time of 1 ms the sensor is ready for I2C. Rule: one 100 nF ceramic directly at the sensor pins with the smallest loop; no bulk cap is datasheet-mandated at the sensor. The sizing subtlety is the heater: DS p9 Table 4 gives measurement current max 500 uA, but supply current with heater on is 60 mA typ / 100 mA MAX at the nominal 200 mW setting. DS p14 heater note 5 states the heater 'draws a large amount of current once enabled (up to ~75 mA in the highest power setting)' and that 'the power supply must be strong enough to avoid large voltage drops that could provoke a sensor reset' - the datasheet's own Table 4 max (100 mA) exceeds the ~75 mA text figure; size for the 100 mA table value. This interacts with the thermal-isolation record's necked-trace rule: a deliberately thin VDD feed onto the sensor island adds resistance, so if firmware will ever run the heater (creep mitigation), check the IR drop of the necked feed at 100 mA plus the regulator's transient response; if the heater is never commanded, the thin feed is unconstrained. Heater duty limit 10 pct, ambient below 65 C for heater use (DS p14).

records.prose: DS p9 Table 4 (read visually): 'Slew rate of the supply voltage' VDD,slew max 20 V/ms, comment: 'Voltage changes on the supply between VDD,min and VDD,max. Faster slew rates may lead to a reset.' Power-up/down threshold VPOR is 0.6-1.08 V static. DS p3: the sensor is ready for I2C at most 1 ms after VDD reaches minimum. The design check this enables: the upstream regulator, load switch or hot-plug edge at the sensor's VDD pin must not traverse the 1.08-3.6 V band faster than 20 V/ms. For a 3.3 V rail that means the ramp from 1.08 V to 3.3 V must take at least (3.3-1.08)/20 V/ms = 111 us. An LDO with soft-start in the hundreds-of-us to ms range passes with margin; a fast load switch or a hot-plugged sensor board (e.g. an SHT4x breakout plugged into a live Qwiic connector, which sees the near-instant cable edge) can violate the limit and leave the sensor reset or hung until re-powered. Action: read the actual startup ramp or soft-start time from the upstream regulator's datasheet and verify >= 111 us equivalent at 3.3 V; slower is always safe - no minimum slew is published. Note this is a supply-quality limit, not a sequencing order requirement: the SHT4x has only VDD/VSS plus the bus, and no enable pin.

records.prose: Each CC pin of a Type-C sink is an independent connection-detection line and shall be terminated on its own. Spec 4.5.2.2.3.1 (Unattached.SNK requirements): "Both CC1 and CC2 pins shall be independently terminated to ground through Rd." Why independence matters: only ONE CC wire runs through a cable; in an electronically marked cable the plug's other CC position carries Ra (0.8 k to 1.2 k, Table 4-26) loading VCONN. Gang CC1+CC2 into one shared Rd and the two detection nodes merge: through an e-marked cable the plug's Ra lands in parallel with the shared Rd, both source-side pins then read SRC.Ra, and per 4.5.2.2.15.2 the source transitions to AudioAccessory when both CC1 and CC2 are SRC.Ra for tCCDebounce. AudioAccessory requirements (4.5.2.2.16.1): "The port shall not drive VBUS" - the board never powers, and only with the better (e-marked, e.g. all 5 A) cables; plain lab cables have no Ra, so the fault ships silently. With two independent Rds the same cable is harmless: Ra parallels only the unused pin's Rd, the CC wire still presents a clean Rd, and the source supplies VBUS. One resistor stuffed instead of two is a dead-board field failure, not a lab failure.

records.prose: The VBUS TVS sits AT the receptacle, on the connector side of the PTC and everything else, so a strike sees the clamp before any series impedance or downstream silicon. SLVA680A p4 (Fig 2-1 models the path as L1..L4 parasitics; summary bullets): place the TVS as near the connector as design rules allow; place the protected IC much farther from the TVS than the TVS is from the connector; no stubs - route directly connector -> TVS -> onward; minimize TVS-to-ground inductance (at 8 kV IEC 61000-4-2 di/dt, 0.25 nH already adds ~10 V, p4 text). P5 (Fig 2-2): the copper between connector and TVS radiates during the strike - keep unprotected traces out of that region and keep corners at 45 deg or gentler. Semtech SI21-03 p3 (Fig 2 on the same page area, full port protection scheme): protection parts hang directly on the port pins, and the VBUS TVS working voltage is chosen against the port's maximum VBUS (22 V class for PD-capable ports). On a 5 V-only sink VBUS reaches at most 5.5 V at light load (spec 4.4.2, p141), so pick stand-off >= 5.5 V (5.0 V nominal parts) with clamp comfortably below the downstream regulator's absolute-maximum input. Ground the TVS into the plane with its own vias next to the connector ground.

- ldo-1117-family-output-cap-esr [feedback] (family/verified, workspace)
  The 1117 class uses the output capacitor as loop compensation, so both a minimum C and an ESR window are requirements. Subject datasheet (AMS1117, Application Hints / Stability, p4): the circuit design "requires the use of an output capacitor as part of the device frequency compensation"; 22 uF solid tantalum "will ensure stability for all operating conditions"; bypassing ADJ raises the requirement and 22 uF tantalum covers all cases; larger values only improve stability. It publishes NO numeric ESR window. TI's LM1117 (same 1117 family) quantifies it (s9.2.2.1.3, p15): minimum 10 uF if tantalum, ESR between 0.3 and 22 ohm, 22 uF tantalum when CADJ is used - disagreement on minimum C (10 vs 22 uF) resolved toward the subject part's own 22 uF blanket figure. A bare X5R/X7R ceramic has mohm-level ESR (AN-1482 s6), far BELOW the 0.3 ohm floor: a "same 22 uF" ceramic substitution can push the loop out of its stable region. Use tantalum / polymer with in-window ESR, or a ceramic plus deliberate series resistance, and re-verify. This board's committed 22 uF tantalum-class output cap is exactly the datasheet path - GROUNDED. Contrast: ceramic- stable CMOS LDOs invert the rule - Diodes AP2112 is "Stable with 1.0 uF Flexible Cap: Ceramic, Tantalum and Aluminum Electrolytic" (p1) with 1 uF X5R/X7R in/out in the typical application (p2 Note 4).

The TI LM1117 sibling makes the requirement explicit: "An input capacitor is recommended. A 10-uF tantalum on the input is a suitable input capacitor for almost all applications" (s9.2.2.1.1, p14), and the Fig 9-3 fixed-regulator example marks its 10 uF tantalum CIN "Required if the regulator is located far from the power supply filter" (p16) - the cap's job is local source impedance, so it sits at the VIN pin and becomes mandatory when upstream bulk is not adjacent. Layout per LM1117 9.5.1 (p17): load-current traces wide (parasitic inductance); VOUT-to-ADJ feedback loop as short as possible; ADJ bypass as close as possible to the IC; and when VIN can be shorted to ground, a diode from VOUT to VIN placed close to the pins diverts the output-cap surge. AMS1117 p4 bounds the same risk: the internal diode absorbs 50-100 A microsecond surges, and the external diode is recommended only with very large COUT (1000-5000 uF) or an input crowbar - not needed at 22 uF scale.

- ldo-output-cap-esr-window-principle [feedback] (principle/verified, workspace)
  The LDO output capacitor is a loop component, not just a reservoir: its ESR forms a zero at f = 1/(2*pi*ESR*Cout). In classic LDOs the loop counts on that zero for phase lead - AN-1482 Fig 4 (gain/phase plot) shows a 10 uF / 0.5 ohm tantalum's 30 kHz zero lifting phase margin from 11 to 68 deg. That is why such parts publish a stable ESR RANGE with two boundaries (Fig 6: an electrolytic-stable LDO's measured stable region, roughly 0.1 to 10 ohm at Cout 4.7 uF across 0-200 mA): too-high ESR puts the zero too low and over-extends bandwidth; too-low ESR pushes the zero past crossover and the loop oscillates. Ceramics have mohm-level ESR (a 10 uF ceramic's zero lands above 3 MHz - s6), so a bare low-ESR ceramic can sit OUTSIDE an ESR-zero part's stable region. Ceramic-stable LDOs instead build the zero into the error amp (Fig 5, series Rcomp): minimum stable ESR drops to ~0 but the MAXIMUM drops too (~0.5 ohm, Fig 7) - the capacitor requirement inverts between the two design eras. Corollary (s7/Fig 8): small 0.01-0.1 uF ceramics sprinkled on the rail add a pole; 1 uF of ceramic bypass dropped a 68 deg margin to 9 deg. Never swap output-cap type against the part's stated stability conditions, and keep stray small ceramics away from the output terminal (s8).

- mcu-decoupling-per-supply-pin-pair [decoupling] (principle/verified, workspace)
  Principle: an MCU draws its supply current in short spikes on clock and I/O edges; spikes cannot be delivered over long supply lines, so the decoupling capacitor is the source - one HF ceramic (100 nF is both vendors' value here) per supply pin pair, placed as close as the package allows so the cap->VDD->VSS->cap loop is minimal, plus one bulk cap per device to stabilize the rail. AN2519 Fig 2-1 (read p.5) draws the failure: a cap placed far away enlarges the high-current loop, the power/ground planes join the loop and the whole ground plane acts as an antenna, raising radiated emission. P.6 (Fig 2-2 read): connect the cap as close as possible to the power and ground pins - for large packages the opposite side of the board may get it closest - it is critical to minimize the loop area between cap and pins; for devices with multiple power/ground pin pairs "there is a decoupling capacitor for every pair of pins"; the main supply "should also have a tantalum or ceramic capacitor to stabilize it". ST states the same for the subject part: DS12991 Fig 9 caution (read p.39) - decouple the supply pin pair with the shown ceramics "as close as possible to, or below, the appropriate pins on the underside of the PCB"; p.70 General PCB design guidelines - the 100 nF must be good-quality ceramic, as close as possible to the chip.

- mcu-internal-rc-accuracy-vs-interface-budget [selection] (family/verified, workspace)
  Crystal-less operation is a budget comparison: the internal RC's total accuracy (trim + temperature + supply drift) against the clock-tolerance budget of each clocked interface. Subject-part numbers, DS12991 Table 38 (read p.54-55): HSI16 factory-trimmed to 15.88-16.08 MHz at 30 C / 3.0 V (-0.75/+0.5 pct); drift +-1 pct over 0..85 C, -2/+1.5 pct over -40..85 C, -0.1/+0.05 pct over VDD; start-up 1.2 us max, stabilization 5 us max. Worst-case sum 0..85 C is about -1.85/+1.55 pct. The UART budget, cross-vendor (AVR16EA DS 25.3.3.2.3, Tables 25-4/25-5, read): the recommended maximum receiver baud-rate error - assuming transmitter and receiver split the total error equally - is +-2.0 pct for a D=8 frame (8N1) in 16x-oversampling mode, tightening to +-1.5 pct at D=10 and in 8x (double-speed) mode. Verdict for the class: an RC-clocked UART at a standard baud rate is acceptable against a crystal-timed link partner over 0..85 C (RC error stays inside the +-2 pct half-budget, with little margin at the extremes); it is marginal at industrial cold (-40 C blows the 8N1 budget on drift alone) and when BOTH ends run on RC (they consume the whole split). Interfaces whose specified clock tolerance is tighter than the RC spec - USB full-speed is the canonical case - are out of reach without a crystal or a closed-loop trim source; not live here (G030 has no USB peripheral). Longer frames (parity, 9-bit) tighten the budget one step.

Floor: UM10204 p50 Eq 2, Rp(min) = (VDD - VOL(max)) / IOL with the spec sink of 3 mA at VOL 0.4 V for VDD > 2 V (Table 10, p43): at 3.3 V that is (3.3-0.4)/3 mA ~ 970 ohm for interop with any compliant device. The SHT4x's own laxer floor is 390 ohm at VDD >= 1.62 V (DS Table 4, p9). Ceiling: UM10204 p50 Eq 1, Rp(max) = tr / (0.8473 x Cb); tr max is 1000 ns Standard, 300 ns Fast, 120 ns Fm+ and Cb max 400 pF (Table 11, p44). Application: Cb is the TOTAL of traces, pins, cable and downstream device, and the ceiling must hold at the TOP of the Cb budget - at 400 kHz Eq 1 is Rp(max)[kohm] ~ 354/Cb[pF]: 2.36 k at 150 pF but only 1.77 k at 200 pF. For a ~0.5 m cable plus one remote node (150-200 pF budget) fit ~1.5 kohm: Eq 1 then holds to ~236 pF, margin over the whole budget, and it stays above the 970 ohm floor (~1.9 mA sink at 3.3 V). Re-derive 354/Cb for a different cable length rather than copying the value; past ~365 pF the 400 kHz window closes against the 970 floor entirely; a 100 kHz-only bus relaxes the ceiling ~3.3x (tr 1000 ns). Fit the pull-ups once, at the host board; do not duplicate them on downstream nodes. Neither Sensirion nor the connector ecosystem publishes a pF/m figure for the Qwiic cable - estimate, then verify rise time at bring-up. DS p3 Fig 1 shows 10 kohm pull-ups: valid only for a short single-device bus, too high once a cable is added.

- sht4x-rht-pcb-conduction-principle [thermal] (principle/verified, workspace)
  PCB copper conduction, not air, is the dominant path carrying board self-heat into an RH/T sensor die. Design Guide sec 3 (p8, read visually): external heat sources raise the sensed temperature and depress the RH reading; in the extreme case at 90 pct RH a 1 degC deviation produces a 5 pct RH error - RH error is ~5x the temperature error at high humidity. Heat conduction from nearby sources (power electronics, microprocessors, displays) is called 'the more severe and most common source of temperature deviations' and 'mostly it occurs through the PCB'. Named mitigations: sufficient distance, removal of unnecessary metal around the sensor (trough milling or etching slits), and keeping metal connections on the PCB as thin as possible. Fig 8 panels: a) thin metal connections + distance = good; b) milled slits (white lines) around the sensor decrease conduction = good; c) thick metal connections = bad; d) heat source in close proximity = bad. DG sec 3.3 (p11): rule of thumb - implement the sensor as isolated from the device and as exposed to the environment as possible, best with ambient airflow; Fig 11 shows the three decoupling options: thin PCB connection tongue, milled slits, or a flex. States mechanism and direction only; nothing bounds it, so it is a principle.

- sht4x-vdd-slew-power-up [sequencing] (topology/verified, workspace)
  DS p9 Table 4 (read visually): 'Slew rate of the supply voltage' VDD,slew max 20 V/ms, comment: 'Voltage changes on the supply between VDD,min and VDD,max. Faster slew rates may lead to a reset.' Power-up/down threshold VPOR is 0.6-1.08 V static. DS p3: the sensor is ready for I2C at most 1 ms after VDD reaches minimum. The design check this enables: the upstream regulator, load switch or hot-plug edge at the sensor's VDD pin must not traverse the 1.08-3.6 V band faster than 20 V/ms. For a 3.3 V rail that means the ramp from 1.08 V to 3.3 V must take at least (3.3-1.08)/20 V/ms = 111 us. An LDO with soft-start in the hundreds-of-us to ms range passes with margin; a fast load switch or a hot-plugged sensor board (e.g. an SHT4x breakout plugged into a live Qwiic connector, which sees the near-instant cable edge) can violate the limit and leave the sensor reset or hung until re-powered. Action: read the actual startup ramp or soft-start time from the upstream regulator's datasheet and verify >= 111 us equivalent at 3.3 V; slower is always safe - no minimum slew is published. Note this is a supply-quality limit, not a sequencing order requirement: the SHT4x has only VDD/VSS plus the bus, and no enable pin.

- usbc-sink-cc-independent-rd-principle [selection] (principle/verified, workspace)

Spec 4.5.2.2.3.1 (Unattached.SNK requirements): "Both CC1 and CC2 pins shall be independently terminated to ground through Rd." Why independence matters: only ONE CC wire runs through a cable; in an electronically marked cable the plug's other CC position carries Ra (0.8 k to 1.2 k, Table 4-26) loading VCONN. Gang CC1+CC2 into one shared Rd and the two detection nodes merge: through an e-marked cable the plug's Ra lands in parallel with the shared Rd, both source-side pins then read SRC.Ra, and per 4.5.2.2.15.2 the source transitions to AudioAccessory when both CC1 and CC2 are SRC.Ra for tCCDebounce. AudioAccessory requirements (4.5.2.2.16.1): "The port shall not drive VBUS" - the board never powers, and only with the better (e-marked, e.g. all 5 A) cables; plain lab cables have no Ra, so the fault ships silently. With two independent Rds the same cable is harmless: Ra parallels only the unused pin's Rd, the CC wire still presents a clean Rd, and the source supplies VBUS. One resistor stuffed instead of two is a dead-board field failure, not a lab failure.

- usbc-sink-vbus-tvs-before-series-element [esd] (topology/verified, workspace)
  The VBUS TVS sits AT the receptacle, on the connector side of the PTC and everything else, so a strike sees the clamp before any series impedance or downstream silicon. SLVA680A p4 (Fig 2-1 models the path as L1..L4 parasitics; summary bullets): place the TVS as near the connector as design rules allow; place the protected IC much farther from the TVS than the TVS is from the connector; no stubs - route directly connector -> TVS -> onward; minimize TVS-to-ground inductance (at 8 kV IEC 61000-4-2 di/dt, 0.25 nH already adds ~10 V, p4 text). P5 (Fig 2-2): the copper between connector and TVS radiates during the strike - keep unprotected traces out of that region and keep corners at 45 deg or gentler. Semtech SI21-03 p3 (Fig 2 on the same page area, full port protection scheme): protection parts hang directly on the port pins, and the VBUS TVS working voltage is chosen against the port's maximum VBUS (22 V class for PD-capable ports). On a 5 V-only sink VBUS reaches at most 5.5 V at light load (spec 4.4.2, p141), so pick stand-off >= 5.5 V (5.0 V nominal parts) with clamp comfortably below the downstream regulator's absolute-maximum input. Ground the TVS into the plane with its own vias next to the connector ground.
